## **Github Repo:**

## Data Loading 

```{r}
library("tidyverse")
library("fpp3")
library("seasonal")

retail_raw <- read_csv("retail_sales_raw.csv")
head(retail_raw)
```

## Time and Tsibbles

Datasets:

The retail_ts dataset contains both seasonally adjusted and non-seasonally adjusted monthly retail sales data from January 1992 until September 2026. The key column in this dataset is series_id, with "Month" as the index variable.

The can_gas dataset contains the levels of monthly Canadian natural gas production (in billions of cubic meters) from January 1960 to February 2005. This dataset has no key variable, with index variable also a monthly variable named "Month", along with the gas production variable "Volume".

```{r}
retail_raw_long <- retail_raw |>
  select(observation_date, RSAFS, RSAFSNA) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(RSAFS, RSAFSNA), names_to = "series_id", values_to = "sales")
head(retail_raw_long)

retail_ts <- retail_raw_long |>
  mutate(Month = yearmonth(observation_date)) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month, key = series_id)
head(retail_ts)

head(canadian_gas)

can_gas <- canadian_gas |>
  select(Month, Volume)
head(can_gas)

can_gas_recent <- can_gas |>
  filter(Month >= yearmonth("1990 Jan"))
head(can_gas_recent)
```

```{r}
can_gas_recent <- can_gas_recent |>
  mutate(year = year(Month),
         month   = month(Month, label = TRUE),
         quarter = quarter(Month))
can_gas_recent |>
  mutate(next_month           = Month + 1,
         same_month_last_year = Month - 12) |>
  head()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
can_gas_q <- can_gas |>
filter(Month <= yearmonth("2004 Dec")) |>
  index_by(Quarter = yearquarter(Month)) |>
  summarize(Volume = sum(Volume))
can_gas_q |> autoplot(Volume)
```

(2.6d) We sum the monthly values for gas production rather than taking the mean, as we are trying to observe the total quantity produced over the period, rather than the average monthly production. In the autoplot, the quarterly series does appear to be seasonal.

```{r}
#| echo: false
retail_ts |>
  autoplot(sales) +
  labs(
    title = "U.S. Retail and Food Services Sales",
    subtitle = "Seasonally adjusted vs. not seasonally adjusted",
    x = NULL, y = "Millions of dollars", color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

(2.7b): In the NSA data, we can observe seasonality in the form of spikes near the end of each year(December), and drops at the beginnigs of the year (January, February). We do not see this pattern in the seasonally adjusted data. The two series do appear to follow the same trend in the long run.

(2.7c)

```{r}
#| echo: false
can_gas |>
  autoplot(Volume) +
  labs(
    title = "Canadian Gas Production",
    x = NULL, y = "Volume, In Billions of Cubic Meters" 
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

(2.7d)

```{r}
#| echo: false
can_gas |>
  autoplot(Volume) +
  labs(
    title = "Canadian Gas Production",
    x = NULL, y = "Volume, In Billions of Cubic Meters" 
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  geom_smooth ()
```

I decided to add a trend line using geom_smooth, in order to more easily display how the series changes over time through the seasonality.

## Transformations

(3.1a) The seasonal swings in our Canadian gas plot do appear to grow as the level of the data increases, particularly towards the middle of the plot. However, as the level of the data raises further towards the end of the plot, the size of the seasonal swings do not appear to grow, and may even decrease.

```{r}
#| echo: false
can_gas <- can_gas |>
  mutate(log_volume = log(Volume))
can_gas |>
  autoplot(log_volume) +
  labs(
    title = "Canadian Gas Production (Log Transformed)",
    x = NULL, y = "Log of Volume, In Billions of Cubic Meters" 
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  geom_smooth ()
```

The shape of the logged graph is different than the regular volume graph, as the level of the graph rises much more in the earlier years and is flatter in the later years on the graph. The seasonal swings do appear smaller, however the swings in the middle are still much more pronounced than the swings in the early and later years. I do not think logs are particularly useful for this graph, as while the seasonal variations do appear smaller, the variations in the middle are still disproportinately large compared to the variations at the ends, and the series is not notably more linear than the original.

```{r}
#| echo: false

retail_nsa <- retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFSNA") |>
  mutate(
    log_sales = log(sales)
  )
retail_nsa |>
  autoplot(sales) +
  labs(
    title = "Non-Seasonally Adjusted Retail Sales",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Sales (Millions of Dollars)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

retail_nsa |>
  autoplot(log_sales) +
  labs(
    title = "Non-Seasonally Adjusted Retail Sales (Log Transformed)",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Log of Sales (Millions of Dollars)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The case for log transformation is stronger in the retail series, as it displays strong seasonality and upwards trend, with the log version of the graph appearing much more linear.

```{r}
can_gas <- can_gas |>
  mutate(
    growth_direct = 100 * difference(Volume)/lag(Volume),
    growth_log = 100 * difference(log_volume)
  )
can_gas |>
  autoplot(growth_direct) +
  labs(
    title = "Canadian Gas Production Growth (Direct)",
    x = NULL, y = "Growth Rate (%)" 
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
can_gas <- can_gas |>
  mutate(
    growth_gap = abs(growth_direct - growth_log)
  )
can_gas |>
  autoplot(growth_gap) +
  labs(
    title = "Canadian Gas Production Growth (Gap Between Direct and Log)",
    x = NULL, y = "Growth Rate Gap (%)" 
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

I feel the approximation is rather good, as the gap between the growth rates is small at most points, despite containing a few larger spikes in their difference.

```{r}
retail_ts <- retail_ts |>
  group_by_key() |>
  mutate(growth_mom = 100 * difference(log(sales))) |>
  ungroup()

retail_ts |>
  autoplot(growth_mom) +
  labs(
    title = "Month-over-Month Growth: SA vs. NSA Retail Sales",
    x = NULL, y = "Growth rate (%)", color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The month-over-month growth rates for the NSA series appear to be much noisier, as it contains the seasonal fluctuations from seasonal spending patterns. The SA series removes this variation, making the underlying monthly changes more apparent, similarly to the differences between the SA and NSA series in problem 2.7b.

## Seasonality

```{r}
retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFSNA") |>
  gg_season(sales) +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal Pattern in NSA Retail Sales",
    y = "Millions of dollars"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFS") |>
  gg_season(sales) +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal Pattern in SA Retail Sales",
    y = "Millions of dollars"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
can_gas |>
  gg_season(log_volume) +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal Pattern in Canadian Gas Production",
    y = "Log of Volume"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The seasonal pattern in the can_gas data appears to describe higer production at the beginning and end of the year, with a dip from lower production in the middle months.

```{r}

can_gas |>
  gg_subseries(log_volume) +
  labs(
    title = "Subseries Plot: Canadian Gas Production",
    y = "log(Volume)"
  )
```

```{r}
retail_nsa_x13 <- retail_ts |>
  filter(series_id == "RSAFSNA") |>
  model(x13 = X_13ARIMA_SEATS(sales)) |>
  components()
retail_nsa_x13 |> autoplot()
```

The seasonal factor appear to be the strongest in December, typically being about 10%-20% above trend. The size of the seasonal swings appears to decrease over time.

```{r}
sa_compare <- retail_nsa_x13 |>
  as_tibble() |>
  select(Month, mine = season_adjust) |>
  left_join(
    retail_ts |>
      filter(series_id == "RSAFS") |>
      as_tibble() |>
      transmute(Month, census = sales),
    by = "Month"
  ) |>
  mutate(pct_diff = 100 * (log(mine) - log(census)))

sa_compare |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Month, y = pct_diff)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "My X-13 Seasonal Adjustment Minus the Census Bureau's",
    x = NULL, y = "Difference (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The difference between my seasonal adjustment and the Census Bureau's appears to be very small, with the difference being less than 1% for most of the series. However, larger differences (over 1%) appear around 2020, likely due to the COVID-19 pandemic's impact on retail sales.

```{r}
can_gas_fit <- can_gas |>
  model(TSLM(log_volume ~ trend() + season()))

report(can_gas_fit)

can_gas_fit |>
  tidy() |>
  select(term, estimate, std.error, statistic, p.value) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

The estimated average monthly growth rate is 0.004, or 0.4% per month. The month with the most significant seasonal effect is January.

```{r}
can_gas_fit |>
  augment() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Month)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = log_volume, color = "Actual")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = .fitted, color = "Fitted")) +
  labs(title = "Linear Trend + Seasonal Dummies Fit: Canadian Gas Production",
       y = "log(Volume)", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The fitted model does well in the capturing the seasonal pattern in the data and the overall trend, however it is not as good at capturing short term fluctuations or areas of the data with less linear progression.

```{r}
can_gas_fit |> gg_tsresiduals()
```

```{r}
can_gas_fit |>
  augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24)
```

At the 5% level, our ljung-box test returns a p-value of 0.00. This indicates that there is significant autocorrelation in the residuals, and that our model is not capturing all of the structure in the data.

## Forecast Evaluation

```{r}
gas_cv_fc <- can_gas |>
  select(Month, Volume) |>
  stretch_tsibble(.init = 240, .step = 1) |>
  model(snaive = SNAIVE(Volume),
        tslm   = TSLM(log(Volume) ~ trend() + season())) |>
  forecast(h = 1)

gas_cv_fc |>
  accuracy(can_gas, measures = list(MAE = MAE, RMSE = RMSE))
```

The dates of the first and last forecasts are January 1980 and February 2005, respectively. The SNAIVE model has a lower MAE and RMSE than the TSLM model, indicating that both errors agree that it is the better model for this data.

```{r}
errs <- gas_cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(as_tibble(can_gas) |> select(Month, actual = Volume),
            by = "Month") |>
  mutate(e = actual - .mean) |>
  select(Month, .model, e) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = e) |>
  na.omit()

forecast::dm.test(errs$snaive, errs$tslm, h = 1, power = 1)
```

The DM statistic is -31.278, and the p-value is essentially 0.00 (\<2.2e-16). This indicates that the SNAIVE model is significantly better than the TSLM model at the 5% level, and we reject the null hypothesis that the two models have equal predictive accuracy.

```{r}
gas_cv_fc <- can_gas |>
  select(Month, Volume) |>
  slide_tsibble(.size = 240, .step = 1) |>
  model(snaive = SNAIVE(Volume),
        tslm   = TSLM(log(Volume) ~ trend() + season())) |>
  forecast(h = 1)

gas_cv_fc |>
  accuracy(can_gas, measures = list(MAE = MAE, RMSE = RMSE))
```

The accuracy of our snaive forecast didn't change much, but the accuracy of our tslm forecast improved significantly. This is likely because the tsl, model is able to use more recent data to make its predictions, which is likely more relevant than older data. The SNAIVE model is not affected by this, as it only uses the most recent observation to make its prediction.

## Reflection

The residual analysis from part 4.4c shows that the linear trend with seasonal dummies model does not fully capture all of our Canadian gas production data. The presence of remaining autocorrelation in the residuals indicates that there is predictable information in the dataset that the model is failing to account for. In part 5, the forecast evaluation displays the importance of allowing for changes in trends over time rather than assuming a constant linear trend, and that the ability to explain seasonality and historical trends in a model does not directly mean it will produce accurate future forecasts. A more effective model could consider more lagged observations and incorporate a more sophisticated way of accounting for trend, rather than just assuming a linear trend.
